list.listitem: NSAID use and Helicobacter pylori infection cause most peptic ulcer disease (PUD). C
Patients with "red flags" () and those with an onset of symptoms after age 55 years require referral for endoscopy. B
H. pylori serologic testing is a cost-effective management strategy in untreated patients with dyspepsia. A

The ACG clinical guideline on the management of H. pylori recommends first-line therapy with bismuth quadruple therapy or concomitant therapy consisting of a PPI, clarithromycin, amoxicillin, and metronidazole. Alternative treatments are listed in .A.
Expect PUD symptoms to resolve within 7 to 14 days of the start of H. pylori eradication therapy. If symptoms persist, consider antibiotic resistance or some other cause. C

background.definition: Peptic ulcer disease (PUD) is characterized by defects in the stomach and/or duodenal mucosa, through the muscularis mucosa, allowing inflammation of the underlying tissue by gastric acid and pepsin.

list.listitem: A total of 6.8% of the US population older than 18 years reported a history of PUD in 2003.
A total of 30% to 40% of the US population is infected with H. pylori.
Helicobacter pylori infection: present in 95% of duodenal and 70% of gastric ulcers.
Chronic use of NSAIDS, including aspirin and COX-2 inhibitors.
H. pylori and NSAIDs are synergistic in increasing the risk of PUD.
Other drugs: corticosteroids, bisphosphonates, potassium chloride, clopidogrel, sirolimus, chemotherapy.
Hypersecretion syndromes: gastrinoma (Zollinger-Ellison), systemic mastocytosis, carcinoid syndrome.
Radiation therapy.
Viral infection: herpes simplex virus, cytomegalovirus.
There is controversy over whether smoking and alcohol significantly affect the incidence of PUD.
The mucosal lining of the stomach and duodenum can handle a normal load of gastric acid (pH 1-2) and pepsin.
H. pylori are spread by human saliva, water, and food. H. pylori bacteria have an outer inflammatory protein and cytotoxin that increases virulence and ulcerogenic potential.

NSAIDS inhibit cyclo-oxygenase and prostaglandins, which blocks their effects of enhancing gastric mucosal protection by stimulating mucus and bicarbonate secretion, epithelial cell proliferation, and increased blood flow.
Disruption of the mucosal lining produces inflammation of underlying tissue, causing bleeding and sometimes perforation of the stomach or duodenum wall.
Counseling older patients about the risk of NSAID use is associated with decreased rehospitalization for PUD (odds ratio [OR] = 0.47) and all-cause mortality (OR = 0.44). B
Use acetaminophen instead of NSAIDs when appropriate, or add a proton pump inhibitor in patients with previous NSAID-related ulcer who are unable to discontinue aspirin or NSAIDs.B
Widespread screening for H. pylori infection because of associated risk of PUD and gastric carcinoma is not currently recommended. B

Patients with a history of documented PUD should have empiric H. pylori eradication therapy without testing. If symptoms persist, patients should undergo active H. pylori testing or upper endoscopy. B

A clinical trial randomized 3298 ICU patients with at least one risk factor for GI bleeding to pantoprazole 40 mg once daily or placebo. They found no difference in mortality but a lower risk of GI bleeding in those receiving the proton pump inhibitor (2.5% vs 4.2%, p <0.05, NNT = 59).B

A Chinese trial randomized 4010 H. pylori positive adults to 2 of 3 treatments: garlic supplementation for 7.3 years, a supplement containing vitamin C, vitamin E and selenium for 7 years, or H. pylori eradication. The vitamin supplements and H. pylori eradication both decreased the likelihood of dying of gastric cancer in this population at very high risk for gastric cancer. It took 22.3 years of follow-up before the study showed a statistically significant benefit, though. B

In older patients taking low dose aspirin who were H. pylori positive, those randomized to HP eradication had fewer peptic ulcer bleeds in the next 2 years (NNT = 238). However, the benefit faded over time.

In patients receiving low dose aspirin who had a history of peptic ulcer and GI hemorrhage, a network meta-analysis of 11 RCTs found that both pantoprazole (0.02) and vonoprazan (RR 0.03) are effective at preventing recurrrence and hemorrhage.
Symptoms that best rule in peptic ulcer are pain relieved by food, pain at night relieved by food, and episodic pain.C
H. pylori serologic testing is a cost-effective and effective strategy for untreated patients with dyspepsia. A

Differential.Differential_Features: No organic cause of PUD-like symptoms, diagnosis of exclusion
Older than 45 years, nausea and vomiting, unexplained weight loss, left upper quadrant mass, anemia
NSAIDS, steroids, digitalis, theophylline, caffeine, nicotine, alcohol
Usually with pulmonary manifestations of sarcoidosis, Wegener's granulomatosis
Usually with distal small intestine involvement
Tuberculosis, Giardia, strongyloidiasis, biopsy to confirm infection
Worse with eating, associated with obesity, caffeine, nicotine, alcohol

list.listitem: The usual onset is in a patient younger than 55 years with risk factors of NSAID use and/or undiagnosed H. pylori infection.

The main PUD symptom is gnawing or burning nonradiating epigastric pain that occurs when the stomach is empty; ie, 2 to 3 hours after meals or at night. It can be relieved by food or antacids. Specific symptoms that increase the likelihood of PUD in patients with dyspepsia include pain relieved by food, nighttime awakening accompanied by relief with food, and episodic pain. The overall physician impression is moderately accurate at identifying dyspeptic patients with PUD (LR+ = 2.2, LR− = 0.45).

Signs and symptoms of complicated ulcer or malignancy ("red flags") are listed in . Patients with any of these symptoms should be referred for prompt or urgent upper endoscopy, depending on the symptoms. See the gastrointestinal hemorrhage (upper, nonvariceal) topic for a more detailed discussion of management.
The risk of serious upper gastrointestinal bleeding or perforation is low (1 per 1000 patients per year) in patients who do not take NSAIDs.
In a recent case-control study, only NSAID use was a risk factor for bleeding in patients with PUD.

Diagnostic upper endoscopy is the most accurate test for diagnosing PUD and active H. pylori infection, but is more costly and invasive, and is recommended only for patients with "red flags" (), patients older than 55 years, and those with persistent symptoms.

The sensitivity of the rapid urease test for the diagnosis of H. pylori when assessed at the time of the index endoscopy for PUD bleeding, can be increase by about 12% to 13% (from 61% to 73%-74%) by increasing the number of biopsy samples from the gastric antrum, or biopsying from the gastric body.

H. pylori serologic testing is a cost-effective and effective management strategy in untreated patients with dyspepsia. H. pylori serologic tests only show exposure, not active infection, and may not be useful in older patients or to confirm cure. Active H. pylori infection can be accurately identified with culture from biopsy, urea breath test, or the stool antigen test.
The urea breath test is more expensive, requires patient preparation, and can be adversely affected by antibiotics, bismuth, and proton pump inhibitors.
The stool antigen test is easy to obtain and accurate, but can be effected by antibiotics, bismuth, and proton pump inhibitors.
Repeat testing by urea breath test, stool antigen, or gastric biopsy is indicated for all treated patients for a test of cure

If proof of eradication is desired by urea breath test or stool antigen, the patient should stop using antibiotics, bismuth and proton pump inhibitors for at least 2 weeks prior to testing. There is no need to stop H2 blockers.

British Society of Gastroenterology guidelines (2022) recommend urgent evaluation of patients with UGI alarm symptoms, such as anyone with dysphagia, or persons 55 years or older with weight loss and either dyspepsia, upper abdominal pain, or reflux. They also recommend urgent evaluation for patients 40 years or older who are either from a region where gastric cancer is common or who have a family history of gastroesophageal cancer. Other alarm symptoms warranting a less urgent evaluation include hematemesis; and in persons 55 years or older, treatment-resistant dyspepsia, dyspepsia, or upper abdominal pain with elevated platelet count, low hemoglobin, nausea or vomiting, or nausea or vomiting with any weight loss, reflux, dyspepsia, or upper abdominal pain.

BSG guidelines (2022) also recommend that as part of the initial evaluation, all patients 55 years or older should have a complete blood count with platelets, those with overlapping irritable bowel symptoms should have celiac serology, and those 60 or older with abdominal pain and weight loss should have an abdominal CT to evaluate for pancreatic cancer. All patients with dyspepsia should be evaluated for the presence of helicobacter pylori (HP) using a stool or breath test, and if the results are abnormal the patient should be treated to eradicate HP. The guidelines recommend against the routine use of gastric emptying tests or 24-hour pH monitoring.

The Maastricht consensus guidelines on the diagnosis of H. pylori, include the folowing: (1) A test-and-treat strategy is appropriate for uninvestigated dyspepsia in younger patients without alarm symptoms; (2) an endoscopy-based diagnostic strategy is an option for patients with dyspepsia when the prevalence of HP infection is low; (3) test for HP infection in patients with peptic ulcer who use aspirin and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs; (4) a urea breath test is the recommended initial test; (5) blood tests should generally be avoided; and (6) bismuth, antibiotics, and proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) should be discontinued for 2 to 4 weeks prior to testing.
A clinical rule that predicts the likelihood of ulcer in dyspeptic patients has been developed. However, it is fairly complex and probably not practical for routine use in the primary care setting.

The Glasgow-Blatchford risk score has been well validated for mortality prediction in patients with upper GI bleeding. ACG guidelines (2021) recommend hospitalization for patients with ulcer bleeding and a Glasgow-Blatchford score >1 point or who otherwise cannot be classified as very low risk (score 0 or 1 points).
The laboratory based C-WATCH risk score predicts the likelihood of rebleeding, angiography, surgery, or death.
A risk score can predict the likelihood of persistent bleeding following endoscopic injection in patients with bleeding peptic ulcer.
The ABC risk score predicts mortality in patients with acute upper or lower GI bleed.
See the algorithm in . Although a cutoff of 55 years is recommended, some research suggests a lower cutoff for men.
Following this algorithm reduces the need for endoscopy, reduces cost, reduces the number of sick days, and produces health outcomes equivalent to early endoscopy.
See for PUD treatment algorithm. B

The ACG clinical guideline on the management of H. pylori recommends first-line therapy with bismuth quadruple therapy or concomitant therapy consisting of a PPI, clarithromycin, amoxicillin, and metronidazole. As antimicrobial resistance is increasing, alternative treatments are listed in .A

If the patient has red flag symptoms for complicated PUD or malignancy (see ), begins to have symptoms when older than 55, or has failed H. pylori eradication therapy, consider gastroenterology referral for prompt endoscopy. B
Patients at risk for ulcer related complications from NSAIDs should take a PPI if they continue to take an NSAID. B

ACG guidelines for bleeding peptic ulcer recommend erythromycin infusion prior to endoscopy, prompt endoscopy with bipolar electrocoagulation, heater probe, and absolute ethanol injection for active bleeding, and PPI after endoscopy. A
If possible, patients with PUD symptoms should stop using NSAIDs, COX-2 inhibitors, and high-dose aspirin. If symptoms resolve, no further treatment is necessary.

If a patient with known H. pylori infection and a history of upper GI bleeding is unable to discontinue using NSAIDs or aspirin, give him or her a proton pump inhibitor to prevent recurrent bleeding. If a patient with the same history is using low-dose aspirin, treat H. pylori infection to significantly decrease the incidence of recurrent bleeding.

A randomized trial found that in patients 60 years and older who were taking low dose aspirin and were HP positive, HP eradication reduced the likelihood of subsequent bleed over 2.5 years (NNT = 238).
Italian guidelines recommend HP eradication in all patients with a history of PUD who are also taking aspirin or an NSAID.
Individualized treatment of H pylori is limited by the fact that antibiotic sensitivity testing is not routinely available locally, necessitating the use of empirical therapies.
ACG guidelines (2021) recommend PPI plus amoxicillin plus clarithromycin plus metronidazle/tinidazole, all bid for 7 to 14 days.

A meta-analysis of 143 studies pubished in 2015 concluded that the following regimes were most effective in eradicating H. pylori: 7 to 14 days of PPI plus amoxicillin plus clarithromycin plus metronidazle/tindazole (up to 94% eradication), 10 to 14 days of standard triple therapy plus probiotics (90%) and 10 to 14 days of PPI plus levofloxacin plus another antibiotic (90%). All treatments were tolerated.

One week of triple therapy (proton pump inhibitor, amoxicillin, clarithromycin) had a similar H. pylori eradication rate as the 14-day course (80%). In this study, the successful eradication of H. pylori after 14 days was lower than the usual rate of 85% or higher that has typically been reported.

Italian guidelines (2022) recommend bismuth based quadruple therapy (bismuth, PPI, tetracycline and metronidazole). Where dual clarithromycin and metronidazole resistance is low the combination of PPI, clarithromycin, amoxicillin, and metronidazole or tinidazole is an option.

In a meta-analysis, sequential therapy with proton pump inhibitor plus amoxicillin for 5 days, followed by proton pump inhibitor, clarithromycin, and tinidazole for 5 days (all given twice daily) had a 93.4% eradication rate and was more effective than standard triple therapy. A single-day therapy was also 95% effective in one study (see ).

If signs and symptoms persist beyond 14 days, consider antibiotic resistance and retreat with levofloxacin 500 mg daily, amoxicillin 1 g twice daily, and a proton pump inhibitor twice daily for 10 days. Or try the NIH Conventional Triple Therapy plus a proton pump inhibitor ().
Another option is the combination of rifabutin, amoxicillin, and omeprazole which was 80% effective.
In patients with bleeding ulcer, ACG guidelines (2021) recommend a high dose PPI for 3 days, followed by PPI twice daily for at least two weeks.
A Cochrane review concluded that giving PPIs prior to endoscopy reduces the need for hemostatic therapy but has an uncertain impact on other outcomes.
Continue proton pump inhibitor use for 4 weeks for duodenal ulcer, 8 weeks for gastric ulcer.

An Expert Review and Best Practice Advice From the American Gastroenterological Association provided several recommendations concerning PPI use, among these included (verbatim):1) Patients at high risk for ulcer-related bleeding from NSAIDs should take a PPI if they continue to take NSAIDs. 2) The dose of long-term PPIs should be periodically reevaluated so that the lowest effective PPI dose can be prescribed to manage the condition. 3) Long-term PPI users should not routinely raise their intake of calcium, vitamin B12, or magnesium beyond the Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA). 4) Long-term PPI users should not routinely screen or monitor bone mineral density, serum creatinine, magnesium, or vitamin B12.

In an RCT, following successful hemostasis of a peptic ulcer, 194 patients at high risk for rebleeding were randomized to vonopraan 20 mg bid x 3 days, then 20 mg qd x 28 days or to high dose PPI with pantoprazole infusion for 3 days followed by omeprazole 20 mg bid for 28 days. Vonoprazan was non-inferior for rebleeding (7.1% vs 10.4%) at 30 days as well as at 3 and 7 days.

A 2024 meta-analysis concluded that vonoprazan, despite costing approximately $600 per month, is no more effective or safe than inexpensive proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) for the treatment and prevention of gastric and duodenal ulcers.

ACG guidelines (2021) recommend endoscopic therapy with bipolar electrocoagulation, heater probe, and absolute ethanol injection for ulcers with active spurting or oozing and those with nonbleeding visible vessels. They also recommend erythromycin infusion prior to endoscopy, and endoscopy within 24 hours of admission for patients with bleeding peptic ulcer.

The ACG 2021 guidelines also recommend high-dose PPI continuously or intermittently for 3 days after endoscopy, and then twice daily oral PPI for the next 2 weeks. Consider repeat endoscopy if there is evidence of recurrent bleeding. In the event of failed endoscopic therapy, transcatheter embolization is recommended.

A small randomized trial (n = 66) found that in patients with recurrent peptic ulcer bleeding, over the scope clips were associted with a lower rate of persistent bleeding (6% vs 42%, p = 0.001, NNT = 3) than usual care with through the scope clips.

516 patients with a high risk UGI bleed (Glasgow-Blatchford score of 14) were randomized to early (within 6 hours) v late (within 24 hours) endoscopy. Patients with persistent hemodynamic instabilty after initial resuscitation were excluded. No differences were noted in 30-day all cause mortality, further episodes of bleeding, duration of hospitalization or the number of patients requiring transfusions.
A randomized trial comparing refeeding 24 vs 48 hours in 209 patients after endoscopic hemostasis found higher rates of bleeding with early refeeding, concluding that it was not non-inferior.

A systematic review identified 9 RCTs and cohort studies with 833 patients with adherent clot randomized to endoscopic or conservative therapy. Endoscopic therapy was associated with less rebleeding (OR 0.41, 95% CI 0.22-0.79), all cause mortality (OR 0.47, 95% CI 0.23-0.95), and need for surgery (OR 0.44, 95% CI 0.21-0.95). However when limited to RCTs only the reduction in overall mortality (OR 0.78, 95% CI 0.24-2.52) and overall rebleeding (7.2% vs 18.5%) were lower but differences were no longer statistically significant.

Surgery is rare today given effectiveness of H. pylori eradication regimens and the potential for postsurgical complications, including postvagotomy diarrhea, dumping syndrome, early satiety, and alkaline reflux gastritis.
Indications for surgery include failure of nonoperative management and suspicion of gastric carcinoma.
Vagotomy with antrectomy or gastric resection (Bilroth I and II) is the standard procedure.

In a 15-year follow-up of one RCT of 75 patients with duodenal ulcers, Roux-en-Y gastrojejunostomy was significantly better than a Billroth II reconstruction on symptoms and endoscopic and histologic findings.

Surgery for gastric or duodenal ulcer perforation is a laparoscopic omental patch followed by an H. pylori eradication regimen; and no significant differences exist in surgical outcomes in patients with perforated peptic ulcer treated with laparoscopic vs open surgery.

Negative prognostic factors for patients undergoing surgery for perforated peptic ulcer include: increased age, comorbidity, preoperative delay over 24 hours, acute renal failure, metabolic acidosis, low serum albumin level, tachycardia, and use of NSAIDs or steroids.
ACG guidelines (2021) recommend hospitalization for patients with a Glasgow-Blatchford score >1 point or who otherwise cannot be classified as very low risk.
Signs and symptoms of complicated ulcer or malignancy (see ) are the primary indication for gastroenterology or surgical referral.
Persistent signs and symptoms of PUD after 14 days of H. pylori eradication therapy are also an indication for referral.

Bleeding from PUD requires upper endoscopy to identify and treat with thermal or argon coagulation, injection of saline or epinephrine, or hemoclipping of the bleeding source. It can be managed with fluid and blood resuscitation and intravenous proton pump inhibitors.

In patients with an acute UGI bleed, a restrictive policy of transfusion (only transfusing patients with a hemoglobin <7 g/dL to a level of 7-9 g/dL) was associated with lower mortality, shorter hospital stays and fewer adverse events than a liberal strategy in which the transfusion threshold was 9 g/dL with a post transfusion goal of 9 to 11 g/dL.
ACG guidelines (2021) also recommend transfusion if the patients hemoglobin is <7 g/dL. A higher threshold may be appropriate in patients with established cardiovascular disease.

Gastric or duodenal penetration or perforation is a surgical emergency. Suspect gastric or duodenal penetration or perforation in a patient with symptoms of PUD associated with an acute abdomen and with free air under the diaphragm on plain abdominal films.

Gastric outlet obstruction is characterized by nausea and vomiting, early satiety, bloating, and weight loss. Endoscopy is indicated, as is measurement of gastric residual volume. Treatment involves correcting the underlying cause with proton pump inhibitors, balloon dilatation, and/or surgery.
Treatment with intermittent PPI therapy is as effective as continuous infusion of PPIs for the prevention of rebleeding in patients with high-risk bleeding ulcers treated endoscopically.
Expect PUD symptoms to resolve within 7 to 14 days of H. pylori eradication therapy. If symptoms persist, consider antibiotic resistance or some other cause. C
The recurrence rate of H. pylori reinfection is 1% to 2% per year.

Patients with co-morbid conditions including hepatic, renal and neoplastic disease have greater 30-day or in-hospital mortality with peptic ulcer bleeding than those without such co-morbitity (RR 4.04-6.03).B
Untreated peptic ulcers have a variable natural history. Some heal spontaneously; others heal then recur within months to 2 years if untreated.
The Glasgow-Blatchford risk score has been well validated for mortality prediction in patients with upper GI bleeding.
The laboratory based C-WATCH risk score predicts the likelihood of rebleeding, angiography, surgery, or death.
The ABC risk score predicts mortality in patients with acute upper or lower GI bleed.
There is usually rapid resolution of PUD symptoms with the cessation of NSAIDs, if appropriate, and after 7 to 14 days of H. pylori eradication therapy.
Successful H. pylori eradication reduces the PUD recurrence rate from 90% to less than 5% per year.
Recurrence of H. pylori infection after successful triple therapy is 1% to 2% per year.

Negative prognostic factors for patients undergoing surgery for perforated peptic ulcer include: increased age, comorbidity, preoperative delay over 24 hours, acute renal failure, metabolic acidosis, low serum albumin level, tachycardia, and use of NSAIDs or steroids.
No follow-up is indicated unless symptoms are refractory to H. pylori eradication, which may represent antibiotic resistance or other cause of PUD.
Ulcers are frequently associated with a type of bacteria called H. pylori and antibiotic therapy is necessary in addition to symptom control.
It is important to finish the entire course of the antibiotic treatment even if you feel better.
Symptoms that require early follow-up include blood in stools or black tarry stools, vomiting, and severe abdominal pain.
If symptoms persist after H. pylori eradication therapy you may need to undergo an endoscopy to get a better understanding of what is causing your symptoms.
Elderly patients may present with painless ulcers or nonspecific complaints.
Gastric carcinoma is more common with an onset of symptoms after age 55 years. Refer for endoscopy if symptoms begin after age 55 years.
The following antibiotics commonly used for H. pylori eradication are safe in pregnancy: clarithromycin (pregnancy risk factor C), metronidazole, and amoxicillin. B
There is no increased risk of congenital malformations, preterm delivery, or growth retardation with the use of proton pump inhibitors (pregnancy risk factor C) or H2 blockers in pregnancy. B
Misoprostol is contraindicated because of its effect on the cervix and uterus.

cell.label: Alarm signs or symptoms present (older than 55 years, anemia, dysphagia, persistent vomiting, gastrointestinal bleeding, involuntary weight loss >5%, jaundice, abdominal mass)?
Potential medications causing dyspepsia (eg, NSAIDs, bisphosphonates, antibiotics)?
Test for H. pylori with urea breath test or stool antigen and treat accordingly. Alternative: empiric proton pump inhibitor only for 4 to 6 weeks. Symptoms resolve?
Appropriate follow-up, consider endoscopy if symptoms recur.

feature.caption: Treatment of Helicobacter pylori-Associated Peptic Ulcer Disease.
feature.feature_body:
Regimen Eradication Rate Duration Notes
PPI plus amoxicillin plus clarithromycin plus metronidazle/tinidazole, all bid 94% 7-14 days Meta-analysis of 143 studies Also recommended by 2021 ACG guideline.
PPI bid + amoxicillin 1 g bid + clarithromycin 500 mg bid plus probiotics 90% 10-14 days Meta-analysis of 143 studies
PPI plus levofloxacin plus another antibiotic, all bid 90% 7-14 days Meta-analysis of 143 studies
PPI bid + amoxicillin 1 g bid + clarithromycin 500 mg bid 80%-90% 7-14 days 7 days vs 14 days had similar eradication. Onlly for patients without macrolide exposure and where macrolide resistance is low.
PPI bid + clarithromycin 500 mg bid + metronidazole 500 mg bid 80%-90% 7-14 days Useful for penicillin allergy
2 tablets of 262 mg bismuth subsalicylate, metronidazole 500 mg, and 2 g amoxicillin suspension, all taken 4 times over the course of the day, along with 60 mg lansoprazole taken once 95% 1 day 1 day regimen—only studied in a single clinical trial
PPI plus 1 g amoxicillin for 5 days followed by PPI, clarithromycin 500 mg and tinidazole 500 mg for 5 days (all given bid) 93.4% 10 days Sequential therapy has good evidence of efficacy
Bismuth (Pepto-Bismol) 2 tablets daily, metronidazole 250 mg daily, tetracycline 500 mg daily (if intolerant allergic may substitute amoxicillin 1 g bid) plus either H2 blocker or PPI daily 75%-85% 14 days NIH Conventional Triple Therapy: Inexpensive, but more complicated. Useful for failed triple therapy and penicillin allergy
NOTE: The recommended duration of PPI therapy is 8 weeks for gastric ulcer and 4 weeks for duodenal ulcer. PPI denotes proton pump inhibitor; bid, twice daily.
